# estimation.noise_id { #wdm.estimation.noise_id }

`estimation.noise_id`

Phase 1: identifying the noise scales from weight-only history.

Historical episodes with no food log cannot tell you anything about your
metabolism -- without the input, the input-output relationship is unidentifiable.
What they *can* tell you, and what phase 2 needs badly, is the answer to two
questions:

1. How much does a single scale reading scatter around the truth?
2. How fast does the underlying trend genuinely wander?

The ratio of those two is what determines how aggressively any filter should
smooth. Guess it wrong in one direction and the estimate chases every salty
dinner; wrong in the other and it takes three weeks to notice a real change.
Estimating it from your own history, rather than adopting a default, is the
entire value of the old data.

The estimator is maximum likelihood on the local linear trend model, with the
likelihood obtained from the filter's prediction-error decomposition:

$$
\ell(\theta) = \sum_{k \,:\, \text{observed}}
-\tfrac12 \left[ \log 2\pi S_k(\theta) + e_k(\theta)^2 / S_k(\theta) \right].
$$

The Gaussian is chosen on evidence: refitting with Student-t innovations
(``trend_filter(..., dof=...)``) lowers the maximized likelihood on the record
so far, and moves variance from the readings into the trend, which makes any
filter built on the result smooth less.

Episodes contribute additively, sharing the noise parameters while each keeps
its own diffuse initial condition. Optimization runs in log coordinates so the
variances stay positive, with gradients from JAX and the search from L-BFGS-B.

## Classes

| Name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| [NoiseIdentification](#wdm.estimation.noise_id.NoiseIdentification) | Fitted noise scales, in kg and kg/day, with approximate standard errors. |

### NoiseIdentification { #wdm.estimation.noise_id.NoiseIdentification }

```python
estimation.noise_id.NoiseIdentification(
    level_sd,
    slope_sd,
    obs_sd,
    level_sd_factor,
    slope_sd_factor,
    obs_sd_factor,
    loglik,
    n_observations,
    n_episodes,
    converged,
    message,
)
```

Fitted noise scales, in kg and kg/day, with approximate standard errors.

Standard errors come from the observed information matrix -- the Hessian of
the negative log-likelihood at the optimum -- and are reported in log units,
then converted to a multiplicative factor. A ``obs_sd`` of 0.45 kg with a
factor of 1.15 means roughly a 68 % interval of ``[0.39, 0.52]``.

Treat them as optimistic. They assume the local linear trend model is
correctly specified, which it is not -- it has no notion of glycogen, sodium,
or a food log. They are useful for judging whether a parameter is pinned
down or merely guessed, and not for much beyond that.

### identify_noise { #wdm.estimation.noise_id.identify_noise }

```python
estimation.noise_id.identify_noise(
    episodes,
    *,
    init=(0.05, 0.005, 0.45),
    min_observations=10,
    dof=None,
)
```

Fit the three noise scales by maximum likelihood.

#### Parameters {.doc-section .doc-section-parameters}

| Name             | Type            | Description                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     | Default    |
|------------------|-----------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|------------|
| episodes         | list\[Episode\] | Episodes to use. All are used, including ones that *do* have food logs: the local linear trend model ignores intake entirely, so a logged episode is simply more weight data. This is deliberate -- more observations make a better noise estimate, and phase 2 re-estimates everything that actually depends on intake anyway. | _required_ |
| min_observations | int             | Refuse to fit below this many total weigh-ins. Three noise scales cannot be identified from a handful of points, and a confident-looking answer from too little data is worse than no answer.                                                                                                                                   | `10`       |
| dof              | float \| None   | Student-t degrees of freedom for the observation noise, or ``None`` for Gaussian. Must match what phase 2 is given.                                                                                                                                                                                                             | `None`     |

### total_loglik { #wdm.estimation.noise_id.total_loglik }

```python
estimation.noise_id.total_loglik(log_theta, arrays, dof=None)
```

Summed log-likelihood across episodes at the given log noise scales.
